docs.title: 🌊 Surf Weather API
docs.text:
Build weather-powered applications using real-time coastal data.

The Surf Weather API gives developers fast, reliable access to current weather conditions for surf and coastal applications — from a single endpoint you can integrate in minutes.

docs.title: Start Building
docs.text: The Surf Weather API provides developers with fast, reliable access to weather data for surf and coastal applications.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Retrieve real-time weather data — current conditions including temperature, wind, humidity, pressure, and human-readable weather descriptions for any coastal city.
  • Query by city or location — pass a city name such as Goa or Bondi Beach and get structured JSON back.
  • Secure API key authentication — every request is authenticated with your personal API key, so usage is tracked and protected.
  • Integrate quickly using SDK examples — copy-paste code samples take you from zero to a working call in under five minutes.

docs.title: Developer Journey
docs.text:
Follow this path to get started quickly:

  1. ➡️ Getting Started — create an account, generate an API key, and set up your environment → developer-docs/getting-started.md
  2. ➡️ Authentication — learn how API key authentication works and how to keep your key safe → developer-docs/authentication.md
  3. ➡️ First API Call — make your first /weather request and understand the response → developer-docs/v1/first-api-call.md
  4. ➡️ SDK Examples — integrate using ready-made code samples → developer-docs/v1/python.md
  5. ➡️ Production Usage — rate limits, error handling, and best practices for going live → developer-docs/rate-limits.md and developer-docs/error-catalog.md

docs.title: About This Project
docs.text: This documentation portal was created as a real-world simulation of startup API documentation. It serves the fictional Surf Weather API — a service providing real-time coastal and surf weather data — and demonstrates how a small team can plan, structure, and maintain developer-facing documentation using a docs-as-code workflow.

docs.title: Project Goal
docs.text:
The goal was to design a developer-first documentation system that demonstrates:

  • API documentation strategy — planning content around what developers actually need, in the order they need it
  • Developer onboarding flow — a guided path from account creation to the first successful API call
  • Versioned documentation architecture — stable (v1) and beta (v2) documentation living side by side
  • Docs-as-code workflow — documentation written in Markdown, versioned in Git, and published like software

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• MkDocs (Material Theme) — static site generator and theme used to build and style the portal
  • Markdown — the authoring format for all guides and reference pages
  • OpenAPI Specification (YAML) — the machine-readable API contract (openapi.yaml) used for interactive testing
  • Git-based workflow — branching, pull requests, and reviews applied to documentation changes

docs.title: Documentation Strategy
docs.text:
The structure follows a developer journey:

  1. Introduction & onboarding
  2. Authentication
  3. First API call
  4. SDK usage
  5. Error handling
  6. Versioned API reference

This reduces friction for new developers: each page answers the question that naturally arises after the previous one, instead of forcing readers to hunt through a flat reference.

docs.title: Versioning Approach
docs.text:
• v1 → Stable production API
  • v2 → Beta / future enhancements

Version folders allow independent evolution of APIs and documentation. Breaking changes ship in a new version folder while the stable version remains untouched, so existing integrators are never surprised.

docs.title: API Reference Approach
docs.text:
Instead of embedding Swagger directly, the documentation links to the OpenAPI specification.

This mirrors many real-world startup practices where:

  • Guides remain lightweight
  • API testing is handled via Swagger Editor or dedicated portals

docs.title: Locations & Search
docs.text:
Why is my location not showing?

Try searching using a nearby city name or check the spelling. Smaller surf spots are sometimes listed under the nearest coastal town. You can also search by region or coordinates.

Can I save multiple locations?

Yes. Click ⭐ on any location to add it to your favorites. Saved locations appear under the search bar, and you can reorder or rename them in Settings → Saved Locations.

docs.title: Data & Forecasts
docs.text:
Why are weather values delayed?

Data refreshes every few minutes depending on provider updates. A timestamp on the dashboard's Current Conditions panel shows when the last update was received.

How far ahead can I see forecasts?

The hourly forecast covers the next 24 hours, and the weekly forecast covers seven days.

Can I change the units (Celsius/Fahrenheit)?

Yes. Go to Settings → Units to switch temperature, wave height, and wind speed units. Changes apply instantly across the app.

docs.title: Account & Login
docs.text:
I cannot log in

  • Verify your email and password
  • Reset your password using "Forgot Password" on the login page
  • Check your internet connection

How do I update my profile details?

Open the profile menu and go to Settings → Profile to change your display name, photo, email address, or password.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Why am I not receiving alerts?

Check that alerts are enabled in Settings → Alerts and that browser/app notification permissions are allowed. See the Troubleshooting guide for detailed steps.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Welcome to Surf Weather.

This guide helps you start using the platform in under 5 minutes. By the end, you will be signed in, viewing live surf conditions for your favorite spot, and have it saved for quick access.

docs.title: Step 1 — Sign In
docs.text:
Log in using your registered email and password.

  1. Open the Surf Weather app or website.
  2. Enter your registered email address and password.
  3. Click Sign In.

New here? Select Create Account on the login page, confirm your email address, and then sign in.

docs.title: Step 2 — Select Location
docs.text:
Use the search bar to find your coastal city or beach.

  1. Click the search bar at the top of the dashboard.
  2. Type a spot name, city, or region — for example, Goa or Bondi Beach.
  3. Pick the correct result from the suggestions.

The dashboard reloads immediately with data for the selected location.

docs.title: Step 3 — View Surf Conditions
docs.text:
The dashboard displays:

  • Wave height — current significant wave height
  • Wind speed — including direction, so you can judge onshore vs. offshore conditions
  • Temperature — air and water temperature
  • Tide levels — current tide state and the next tide change

Scroll down for the hourly forecast (next 24 hours) and the weekly outlook. See the User Manual for a full tour of the dashboard.

docs.title: Step 4 — Save Favorite Locations
docs.text:
Click ⭐ to save locations for quick access later.

  • Saved locations appear under the search bar for one-tap switching.
  • Your top favorite becomes the default dashboard view when you sign in.
  • Favorites sync across devices linked to your account.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
• Set up alerts for high waves, strong winds, and storm warnings — see the User Manual
  • Something not working? Check the Troubleshooting guide
  • Building with the API instead? Start with Getting Started

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Use this guide to resolve the most common issues. Each problem lists likely causes and step-by-step solutions.

docs.title: Problem: Dashboard not loading
docs.text:
Possible causes

  • Slow internet connection
  • Temporary server delay
  • Corrupted browser cache

Solution

  1. Refresh the page.
  2. Clear browser cache.
  3. Try again after a few minutes.
  4. If the problem persists, try a different browser or device to isolate the issue.

docs.title: Problem: No weather data displayed
docs.text:
Possible causes

  • Invalid location
  • Data provider delay

Solution

  1. Select another nearby location.
  2. Check again after refreshing.
  3. Confirm the location name against a nearby coastal city if the spot is small or newly added.

docs.title: Problem: Alerts not working
docs.text:
Possible causes

  • Alerts disabled in settings
  • Notification permissions blocked

Solution

  1. Go to Settings → Alerts.
  2. Enable notifications.
  3. Allow browser notifications.
  4. Verify the alert thresholds — alerts only trigger when conditions exceed the values you set.

docs.title: Problem: Cannot log in
docs.text:
Possible causes

  • Incorrect email or password
  • Unconfirmed account

Solution

  1. Re-enter your credentials carefully (watch for caps lock).
  2. Use Forgot Password to reset your password.
  3. Check your inbox (and spam folder) for the account confirmation email.

docs.title: Problem: Units or settings not saving
docs.text:
Possible causes

  • Changes not saved before leaving the page
  • Browser blocking cookies or local storage

Solution

  1. Click Save before navigating away from Settings.
  2. Allow cookies and local storage for the Surf Weather site.
  3. Sign out and back in to force a settings sync.

docs.title: Before You Contact Support
docs.text:
To help us resolve your issue faster, please include:

  • The email address on your account
  • The location(s) affected
  • A screenshot of the problem, if possible
  • The browser and device you are using

docs.text:

docs.title: User Manual
docs.text: This manual explains all major features available to users. It walks you through the dashboard, location search, alerts, and account settings, with step-by-step instructions and tips for getting the most out of the app.

docs.title: Dashboard Overview
docs.text: The dashboard is the first screen you see after signing in. It provides real-time surf and weather insights for your currently selected location, combining live observations with forecast data so you can plan your session at a glance.

docs.title: Current Conditions
docs.text:
The Current Conditions panel shows what is happening right now at your selected location:

  • Wave height — the current significant wave height, displayed in feet or meters depending on your unit settings
  • Swell direction and period — where the swell is coming from and the seconds between waves; longer periods generally mean more powerful, better-organized surf
  • Wind speed and direction — onshore winds typically make conditions choppy, while light offshore winds groom the waves
  • Air and water temperature — so you can pick the right wetsuit or rash guard
  • Tide state — whether the tide is rising, falling, or at high/low slack, along with the time of the next tide change

Data in this panel refreshes automatically every few minutes. A timestamp at the bottom of the panel shows when the last update was received.

docs.title: Hourly Forecast
docs.text:
The Hourly Forecast panel shows expected conditions hour by hour for the next 24 hours. Scroll horizontally to move through the timeline. Each hour displays wave height, wind, and a condition rating so you can quickly spot the best window — for example, a morning glass-off before the wind picks up at midday.

Tap any hour to expand it and see full detail, including swell period, tide height, and precipitation probability.

docs.title: Weekly Forecast
docs.text:
The Weekly Forecast panel extends the outlook to seven days. Each day is summarized with:

  • Expected wave height range (minimum to maximum)
  • Dominant swell direction
  • Wind trend for the day
  • An overall condition rating (Poor, Fair, Good, or Epic)

Use this view to plan ahead — for instance, spotting a swell arriving midweek so you can arrange time off in advance.

docs.title: Alerts Panel
docs.text: The Alerts Panel sits at the top of the dashboard whenever an active alert applies to your location. It shows all triggered alerts — such as high waves or storm warnings — with their severity level and expiry time. See the Alerts section below for setup details.

docs.title: Location Search
docs.text:
Use the search bar at the top of the dashboard to switch between locations.

To change your location:

  1. Click or tap the search bar.
  2. Type the name of a beach, surf spot, or coastal town — suggestions appear as you type.
  3. Select a result from the list. The dashboard immediately reloads with data for the new location.

Tips:

  • You can search by spot name ("Pipeline"), region ("North Shore Oahu"), or coordinates.
  • Recently viewed locations appear below the search bar for one-tap access.
  • Save frequently used spots to your favorites (see Account Settings) so they sync across your devices.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Alerts notify you when conditions at your saved locations meet thresholds you care about, so you never miss a good session — or get caught out by dangerous weather.

Users can enable alerts for:

  • High waves — triggered when wave height exceeds a limit you set (for example, notify me when waves go above 6 ft). Useful both for chasing big swells and for safety warnings.
  • Strong winds — triggered when sustained wind speed passes your chosen threshold, warning you of blown-out conditions or hazardous offshore winds.
  • Storm warnings — triggered automatically when official meteorological services issue a storm, cyclone, or severe weather advisory for one of your saved locations. These cannot be disabled, as they are safety-critical.

To configure alerts:

  1. Open the profile menu and select Alerts.
  2. Choose the saved location the alert applies to.
  3. Toggle on the alert types you want.
  4. For high waves and strong winds, set your preferred threshold values.
  5. Choose how you want to be notified — push notification, email, or both.

Active and recently expired alerts remain visible in the dashboard's Alerts Panel until they are dismissed.

docs.title: Account Settings
docs.text: From the profile menu in the top-right corner, you can manage everything related to your account.

docs.title: Change Units (Celsius/Fahrenheit)
docs.text:
Switch between metric and imperial units at any time:

  1. Open the profile menu and select Settings.
  2. Under Units, choose your preference for temperature (Celsius/Fahrenheit), wave height (feet/meters), and wind speed (knots, km/h, or mph).
  3. Changes apply instantly across the dashboard, forecasts, and alerts.

docs.title: Manage Saved Locations
docs.text:
Your saved locations (favorites) are listed under Settings > Saved Locations. From here you can:

  • Add a new location using the search bar
  • Reorder the list by dragging — the top location becomes your default dashboard view
  • Remove locations you no longer need
  • Rename locations with custom labels (for example, "Home break" or "Holiday spot")

docs.title: Update Profile Details
docs.text:
Under Settings > Profile you can:

  • Change your display name and profile photo
  • Update the email address associated with your account
  • Change your password
  • Manage notification preferences and connected devices

Remember to save your changes before leaving the page. If you update your email address, you will receive a confirmation link at the new address — your settings take effect once you confirm.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: All API requests require an API key. Requests without a valid key are rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.

docs.title: How to Get an API Key
docs.text:
1. Create an account on the provider's website.
  2. Open your account dashboard and navigate to the API Keys section.
  3. Click Generate New Key, give it a recognizable name (for example, mobile-app-prod), and copy it.
  4. Store the key securely — treat it like a password.

docs.title: Authentication Method
docs.text:
Authentication is performed using query parameters. Append your key as the appid parameter on every request.

Example:

https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Goa&appid=YOUR_API_KEY

docs.title: Using Environment Variables
docs.text:
Avoid hard-coding your key. Load it from the environment instead:

export WEATHER_API_KEY="your_key_here"

import os
api_key = os.environ["WEATHER_API_KEY"]

This keeps secrets out of source control and makes key rotation painless.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Never expose API keys publicly — keep them out of Git repositories, tickets, and screenshots
  • Store keys in environment variables — or a secrets manager in production
  • Rotate keys periodically — revoke old keys after rotation and audit usage in your dashboard

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text: Code Meaning What to do 401 Invalid API key Verify the key is correct, active, and passed as appid; check for extra whitespace when copying

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: ➡️ Continue to First API Call

docs.title: Error Catalog
docs.text: This page lists common API errors and resolutions. All errors are returned as standard HTTP status codes; log them during development so failures are easy to diagnose.

docs.title: Error Reference
docs.text: Code Description Resolution 400 Bad request Verify parameters — a required parameter such as q is missing or malformed 401 Unauthorized Check API key — confirm it is correct, active, and passed as the appid query parameter 404 Not found Verify endpoint — check the URL path spelling, and confirm the city name exists (try a nearby larger city) 429 Rate limit exceeded Retry later — wait for the rate-limit window to reset, and implement exponential backoff (see Rate Limits) 500 Server error Retry or contact support — if the error persists for more than a few minutes, reach out to support@surfweather.com

docs.title: Handling Errors in Code
docs.text:
Always check the status code before parsing the response body:

response = requests.get(url, params=params)

if response.status_code == 200:
    data = response.json()
elif response.status_code == 401:
    raise RuntimeError("Invalid API key — check your appid parameter")
elif response.status_code == 429:
    raise RuntimeError("Rate limited — back off and retry")
else:
    response.raise_for_status()

docs.title: Debugging Tip
docs.text: Always log response status codes during development. Pair the status code with the request URL (with the API key masked) so you can reproduce failing calls quickly.

docs.text:

  • Rate Limits — avoiding 429 errors

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Welcome to the Surf Weather API.

This guide helps you make your first successful API request. By the end, you will have an account, an API key, and a working setup ready for your first call.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin:

  • Create an OpenWeather account — sign up at the provider's website with your email address
  • Generate an API key — from your account dashboard, create a new key and copy it somewhere safe; it is only shown in full once
  • Install a REST client — Postman for a graphical interface, or curl for the command line

docs.title: Base URL
docs.text:
All API requests are made to:

https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5

The current version (v1) exposes a single endpoint:

  • GET /weather — current weather by city name

docs.title: Make Your First Request
docs.text:
With your API key ready, call the /weather endpoint with a city name:

https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Goa&appid=YOUR_API_KEY

A successful call returns a JSON payload with the current weather description, temperature, wind, and more. For a full walkthrough of the request and response, see First API Call.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Never expose API keys publicly — do not commit them to Git or embed them in client-side code
  • Store keys in environment variables — for example, export WEATHER_API_KEY=your_key_here
  • Rotate keys periodically — generate a new key on a regular schedule and revoke the old one

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
Code Meaning What to do 401 Invalid API key Check that your key is correct and active; confirm you passed it as the appid parameter

For the full list, see the Error Catalog.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: ➡️ Continue to First API Call

docs.title: Rate Limits
docs.text: Rate limits prevent API abuse and ensure stability. They cap how many requests your API key can make within a given time window, keeping the service fast and reliable for everyone.

docs.title: Typical Limits
docs.text:
Plan Requests Free Tier Limited requests per minute (suitable for development and testing) Paid Tier Higher request limits (suitable for production applications)

Exact quotas depend on your subscription — check your account dashboard for current limits and usage.

docs.title: What Happens When You Exceed the Limit
docs.text: Requests beyond your quota receive a 429 Too Many Requests response. The limit resets at the start of the next window, so you can resume calling after a short wait.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Cache responses where possible — current conditions change every few minutes, so caching a response for 5–10 minutes drastically cuts request volume
  • Avoid polling too frequently — request data only when you need it, not on a fixed rapid loop
  • Implement retry logic — when you receive a 429, back off exponentially (wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s…) instead of retrying immediately
  • Batch location lookups — if your app tracks many spots, stagger the calls rather than firing them all at once
  • Monitor your usage — keep an eye on the dashboard so you can upgrade before hitting the ceiling

docs.text:

  • Authentication: see Authentication

docs.title: First API Call
docs.text: This tutorial walks you through your first request to the Surf Weather API. By the end, you will have retrieved current weather data for a city and understood the response.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Make sure you have:

  • An API key (see Authentication)
  • A REST client such as Postman, or curl on the command line

docs.title: Example Request
docs.text:
Replace YOUR_API_KEY with your actual key:

https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Goa&appid=YOUR_API_KEY

Using curl:

curl "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Goa&appid=YOUR_API_KEY"

docs.title: Request Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Location Required Description q query Yes City name — for example, Goa appid query Yes Your API key

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body:

{
  "weather": [
    {
      "description": "clear sky"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Understanding the Response
docs.text:
• weather — an array of condition objects for the location
  • description — a human-readable summary of current conditions (for example, clear sky, scattered clouds, light rain)

The full payload includes additional fields such as temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind. See the OpenAPI specification for the complete schema.

docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 response Invalid or missing API key Verify the appid parameter — see Authentication 404 response City not found Check the spelling of q, or try a nearby larger city 429 response Too many requests Slow down — see Rate Limits

docs.title: Python SDK Example
docs.text: This page demonstrates how to call the Surf Weather API from Python using the requests library.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.8 or later
  • The requests library:
pip install requests
  • An API key stored in an environment variable (see Authentication):
export WEATHER_API_KEY="your_key_here"

docs.title: Example Code
docs.text:
This snippet demonstrates how to fetch current weather data for Goa using the Python requests library.

import os
import requests

url = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather"
params = {
    "q": "Goa",
    "appid": os.environ["WEATHER_API_KEY"]
}

response = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
response.raise_for_status()

data = response.json()
print(data)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Load the key from the environment — os.environ["WEATHER_API_KEY"] keeps the secret out of your source code.
  2. Build the request — the params dict is URL-encoded automatically by requests.
  3. Set a timeout — timeout=10 prevents your script from hanging on a stalled connection.
  4. Check for errors — raise_for_status() throws an exception on 4xx/5xx responses so failures never pass silently.
  5. Parse the JSON — response.json() converts the payload into a Python dictionary.

docs.title: Sample Output
docs.text: {'weather': [{'description': 'clear sky'}]}

docs.title: API v2 Overview
docs.text:
🟡 Status: Beta

API v2 is the next generation of the Surf Weather API. It is under active development and is not recommended for production use — schemas and behavior may change without notice.

docs.title: Planned Improvements
docs.text:
• Improved response consistency — a uniform envelope for all endpoints, with predictable field naming and data types across responses
  • Extended forecast data — hourly and multi-day forecast endpoints beyond the current-conditions data available in v1
  • Better error messaging — structured error bodies with machine-readable codes and human-readable details, replacing plain status-only failures

docs.title: Trying the Beta
docs.text:
1. Review the planned changes above and confirm your integration can tolerate breaking changes.
  2. Test against v2 in a development environment only.
  3. Report issues and feedback to support@surfweather.com — beta feedback directly shapes the stable release.

docs.title: Migration from v1
docs.text:
When v2 reaches stable, a migration guide will be published here covering:

  • Endpoint and schema changes
  • Authentication differences (if any)
  • Deprecation timeline for v1

Until then, continue using API v1 for all production traffic.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: v2 is under active development. Check this page and the Changelog for updates.
